tips.tip: A slight bow is a courteous greeting; if you shake hands, support your right forearm with your left hand, and bow when departing.
tips.why: Bowing is the traditional Korean greeting, shaped by etiquette’s emphasis on respect and social hierarchy; a handshake may accompany it.
tips.evidence: The bow is the traditional Korean greeting, although it is often accompanied by a handshake among men.

tips.tip: Keep a respectful distance and avoid familiar touching, such as pats or back slaps, unless your hosts signal otherwise.
tips.why: Respectful interaction in Korea includes attention to personal boundaries, though closeness and customs can differ by relationship and context.

tips.tip: Use polite forms of address and speech, and follow your host’s lead on names and titles.

tips.evidence: Speakers use honorifics to indicate their social relationship with the addressee and/or subject of the conversation concerning their age, social status, gender, degree of intimacy, and situational context.

tips.tip: It is considered more courteous not to lift your rice bowl to your mouth; leave bowls and dishes on the table.
tips.why: The described dining convention keeps bowls on the table during meals, distinguishing this practice from some neighboring dining customs.
tips.evidence: During a meal, bowls and dishes remain on the table.

tips.tip: Avoid placing chopsticks upright in rice or holding the spoon and chopsticks together in one hand, particularly when dining with elders.
tips.why: Upright chopsticks evoke food offerings at graves, while using the utensils together in one hand is described as poor etiquette around elders.
tips.evidence: Chopsticks may be put down on a table or on a purpose designed chopstick rest, but never put into food standing up

tips.tip: Pay attention to others’ glasses, and if pouring a drink, offer it respectfully with both hands.
tips.why: Reciprocal pouring is part of shared hosting and dining practice; two hands convey respect when a guest pours for someone.
tips.evidence: When adult guests are asked to pour a drink, they are expected to offer the drink respectfully with two hands.

tips.tip: If you need to blow your nose, excuse yourself from the table or do so discreetly.
tips.why: Courtesy at meals includes keeping potentially distracting personal actions from the shared table.
tips.evidence: If such an action is necessary, it is recommended to leave the table or otherwise be discreet.

args.closing: Thank you for flying with us, dear traveler; your hosts’ own guidance is always the finest compass.

args.greeting: Welcome aboard, dear traveler; let us prepare you for a warm introduction to your friend’s family in Japan.
args.title: Meeting your friend’s parents in Japan

tips.tip: Offer a warm, attentive greeting; a modest bow is a thoughtful way to show respect.
tips.why: Bowing is an established social gesture that expresses respect, and its forms range from casual to formal.
tips.evidence: Bowing in Japan (お辞儀, Ojigi) is the act of lowering one's head or the upper part of the torso, commonly used as a sign of salutation, reverence, apology or gratitude

tips.tip: If you know the time-appropriate greeting, use it; a friendly, energetic greeting is appreciated.
tips.why: Greetings are treated as an important part of social interaction, with different phrases used at different times of day.
tips.evidence: Greetings are considered to be of extreme importance in Japanese culture.

tips.tip: Follow your hosts’ lead at the entrance and remove your shoes when entering the home.
tips.why: Removing shoes at the genkan helps keep soil and dust from entering the home; slippers may be offered instead.
tips.evidence: Shoes are never worn inside the home – this ensures that the floor is not stained by soil, sand or dust

tips.tip: If a meal is served, say “itadakimasu” before eating and “gochisōsama deshita” afterward, if comfortable doing so.
tips.why: These expressions mark gratitude for the food and for those involved in preparing it.
tips.evidence: Meals in Japan traditionally begin with the word itadakimasu (いただきます, lit. 'I humbly receive').

tips.tip: At a shared meal, avoid passing food directly from one pair of chopsticks to another.
tips.why: This gesture is associated with the handling of bones after cremation, so another serving method is more considerate.
tips.evidence: it is considered particularly taboo to pass food from chopsticks to chopsticks

tips.tip: If you bring a small gift, offer it graciously and let your hosts decide whether to open it then.
tips.why: Receiving a gift can carry a sense of obligation, and recipients may defer opening one rather than ask to do so.
tips.evidence: Many people will ask a guest to open a gift, but if they do not, the recipient will resist the urge to ask if they can open the gift.

tips.tip: If you are invited to sit on tatami, remove footwear before stepping onto it and follow your hosts’ seating cues.
tips.why: Tatami can be damaged by footwear, and seating customs differ between traditional floor seating and Western-style tables.
tips.source_title: Customs and etiquette in Japanese dining
tips.evidence: shoes or any type of footwear are always taken off when stepping on tatami floors.

args.closing: I wish you a pleasant visit, dear traveler; your hosts’ own guidance will be the best compass.

tips.tip: Offer a small bow when greeting or thanking someone, following the other person's lead in formality.

tips.tip: It is considered more courteous not to leave chopsticks standing vertically in a bowl of rice.

tips.evidence: this behaviour, which is called Tate-bashi (たて箸; たてばし), resembles incense sticks

tips.tip: When sharing food from a communal dish, use the clean end of your chopsticks or a separate serving pair.

tips.evidence: one should turn the chopsticks around to touch the food; it is considered more sanitary.

tips.tip: At a group toast, wait until everyone is served and the toast is made before drinking.
tips.why: The meal custom treats drinking as a shared moment, with the toast marking when the group begins.
tips.source_title: Customs and etiquette in Japanese dining
tips.evidence: Do not start drinking until everybody is served and has finished the toast.

tips.tip: If invited into a home, remove your shoes at the entrance and follow your host's lead about slippers.
tips.why: Removing outdoor footwear helps keep soil, sand, and dust from the home's floors; homes commonly provide indoor slippers.

tips.tip: At a meal, say “itadakimasu” before eating and “gochisōsama deshita” afterward to express thanks.
tips.why: These phrases express gratitude to those who provided and prepared the food, including its ingredients and producers.
tips.evidence: Meals in Japan traditionally begin with the word itadakimasu (いただきます, lit. 'I humbly receive').

tips.tip: Avoid sticking chopsticks upright in rice or passing food directly from chopsticks to chopsticks.
tips.why: Upright chopsticks resemble incense placed in offerings for the dead, while passing food this way recalls the handling of bones after cremation.
tips.source_title: Customs and etiquette in Japanese dining
tips.evidence: Chopsticks are never left sticking vertically into rice, as this behaviour, which is called Tate-bashi (たて箸; たてばし), resembles incense sticks

tips.tip: When sharing food, use the clean end of your chopsticks or a separate serving utensil, especially outside close-family settings.
tips.why: Using a clean utensil for shared dishes is considered more sanitary; the practice may be more relaxed among family or close friends.
tips.source_title: Customs and etiquette in Japanese dining
tips.evidence: When taking food from a communal dish, unless with family or very close friends, one should turn the chopsticks around to touch the food

tips.tip: Wait until everyone is served and the toast is made before drinking; in company, be ready to pour for others rather than yourself.
tips.why: A shared “kanpai” marks the start of drinking, and pouring for one another is part of the described group custom.
tips.source_title: Customs and etiquette in Japanese dining
tips.evidence: Do not start drinking until everybody is served and has finished the toast.

tips.tip: If invited into a home, remove your shoes at the entrance and follow your host’s lead about indoor slippers.
tips.why: Removing outdoor footwear helps keep floors free of soil, sand, and dust; homes commonly have an entry area for this purpose.
tips.evidence: Shoes are never worn inside the home – this ensures that the floor is not stained by soil, sand or dust

tips.tip: At a public bath, wash and rinse thoroughly before entering the shared tub.
tips.why: The tub is for relaxing rather than washing, and its water is kept for other bathers’ use.
tips.evidence: Therefore, the body must be cleaned and scrubbed before entering the bathtub or ofuro.

args.closing: I wish you a most rewarding stay, dear traveler, and your host’s guidance should always come first.

verdicts.reason: Excerpt identifies bowing as a customary greeting and sign of reverence.
Excerpt supports saying itadakimasu, but says nothing about the closing phrase.
Excerpt supports avoiding upright chopsticks, but not passing food between chopsticks.
Excerpt recommends turning chopsticks around when serving oneself from communal dishes.
Excerpt supports waiting for the toast, not pouring drinks for others.
Excerpt supports removing shoes indoors, but not entryway or slipper guidance.
Excerpt says to clean and scrub before entering the bathtub.
